title: An Inspector Calls: plot and structure
specPoints: Paper 2 Section A: modern drama, An Inspector Calls

tips.title: The order is the argument
tips.body: Birling, Sheila, Gerald, Mrs Birling, Eric: the order in which they met the girl, and the order the Inspector takes them. Learn it as a sentence and every plot question, and every essay on responsibility, starts from it.

tips.title: Where the curtains fall
tips.body: Act 1 ends on the name Daisy Renton, Act 2 on the realisation about Eric, Act 3 on the telephone. An essay that knows where the acts end can write about structure; one that only knows what happens can only retell.

tips.title: Two dates, one line of irony
tips.body: Set in 1912, written in 1945. Whenever Birling forecasts the future, the audience knows he is wrong, and that is dramatic irony you can name in one sentence without any further evidence.

tips.title: Three names, three doors
tips.body: Eva Smith at the works and at Milwards, Daisy Renton with Gerald, Mrs Birling at the committee. If you cannot say which name goes with which link, re-read Act 2: the names are how the Inspector, and the audience, join the links.

tips.title: Doubt comes after the exit
tips.body: Nobody questions whether Goole is real while he is on stage. The speech is heard straight, and the wriggling begins only once he has gone. If a question asks about the ending, start from that ordering.

why.matters: A play is built, and the build is where its meaning lives. Priestley chose one room, one evening and continuous time; he chose to take five people in the order they met the girl; he chose to raise the doubt about the Inspector only after the speech had been heard, and to end with a telephone that starts the evening again. Each of those choices does something to an audience that a summary of the story cannot. The exam pays for this directly: twelve of the thirty marks are for the writer's methods, and structure is a method. A student who knows the plot can retell it; a student who knows the build can argue with it.

examples.title: The detective story you already know
examples.body: Every whodunnit works by the same trick Priestley borrows: suspects questioned one at a time, a secret admitted before the next is opened, and a last scene that overturns what everyone thought. Agatha Christie's *The Mousetrap*, which opened in London in 1952, has been running on exactly that engine for more than seventy years. Priestley's variation is that the detective may not be real and the crime is shared by all of the suspects.

examples.title: A twist that starts the story again
examples.body: Television series end seasons the way Priestley ends Act 3: the problem the characters thought was solved comes back in the last thirty seconds, so that the audience wants the next instalment. The telephone in the Birlings' hall does the same job, with one difference. There is no next episode, so the audience is left to imagine the family living the evening again, which is the point.

steps.title: One evening in 1912
steps.body:
Everything in *An Inspector Calls* happens in one room, on one evening, in the spring of 1912. The room is the dining room of the Birlings' house in Brumley, an industrial town in the north Midlands that Priestley invented. Arthur Birling, a manufacturer who has been Lord Mayor, his wife Sybil, their daughter Sheila and their son Eric are finishing dinner with Gerald Croft, the young man from a richer family whom Sheila has just agreed to marry.

That is the whole cast except for two people. One is the maid. The other is the Inspector, whose ring at the door will turn a celebration into an inquiry.

**Two dates to hold at once.** The play is set in 1912, but Priestley wrote it in 1945, the year the Second World War ended, and it was performed first in Moscow and Leningrad that year and in London in October 1946. The audience watching it knew everything that would happen to the world after 1912: the Titanic, two world wars, the strikes and the slump. The characters know none of it. That gap is the play's first structural device, and it is working before the Inspector has even arrived.

steps.title: Act 1: the speech, the doorbell, the photograph
steps.body:
The play opens on comfort and confidence. Birling makes a speech. He is “I speak as a hard-headed business man” (Mr Birling, Act 1), and he tells the young people that there will be no war, that the Titanic is “Unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable”, and that a man should look after himself. Eric's “What about war?” is brushed aside. The doorbell rings in the middle of Birling's certainty, and the Inspector is shown in.

**Inspector Goole** says a young woman, Eva Smith, has died in the Infirmary after drinking disinfectant. He has a photograph, and he shows it to one person at a time.

**Birling's link.** Eva Smith worked at his works. She helped lead a strike for higher wages; when it failed he sacked her. He sees no connection between that and her death.

**Sheila's link.** Eva's next job was at Milwards, the shop. Sheila, in a temper and jealous, had her dismissed. Unlike her father she is shaken: “I'll never, never do it again to anybody” (Sheila, Act 1). The Inspector then says that the girl changed her name to Daisy Renton, and Gerald's reaction to that name tells Sheila, and the audience, that he knew her: the act closes on that discovery.

rows: No war; the Titanic; look after yourself
Every prediction the audience knows to be wrong
The Inspector interrupts the confidence, not the meal
Shown to one person at a time
The first link in the chain
The first confession that admits harm

check.prompt: Which shop did Sheila have Eva Smith dismissed from?
check.solution: Milwards, the shop where Eva Smith found work after Birling sacked her. Sheila had her dismissed out of jealousy and bad temper, and it is the first link in the chain that the person who forged it regrets.

steps.title: Act 2: Gerald, then Mrs Birling
steps.body:
**Gerald's link.** He met Daisy Renton in the bar of the Palace, the local music hall, took her out of it, installed her in a friend's rooms, and kept her through the summer before ending it. Sheila listens to all of it and hands back her engagement ring. Birling reminds the Inspector that he is a public man; the reply is that “Public men, Mr Birling, have responsibilities as well as privileges” (the Inspector, Act 2).

**Mrs Birling's link.** The girl, pregnant, came to the women's charity committee that Mrs Birling chairs, and gave her name as Mrs Birling. That offended her, and she used her influence to have the appeal refused. Questioned, she is unmoved: “I did nothing I'm ashamed of” (Mrs Birling, Act 2), and the father of the child should be made to answer for it, because “It's his responsibility” (Mrs Birling, Act 2).

Sheila had warned her mother as she came in, “You mustn't try to build up a kind of wall between us and that girl” (Sheila, Act 2), and sees the trap closing before her mother does. By the end of the act everyone on stage understands that the father is Eric, and Eric walks in.

rows: Kept her over the summer, then ended it
Honest, and ashamed of some of it
Refused help to a pregnant girl
props.title: The two links of Act 2

visuals.alt: A table comparing Gerald and Mrs Birling in Act 2: where each met Eva Smith, what they did, and how each answers the Inspector

check.prompt: What name did the pregnant girl give when she asked Mrs Birling's committee for help?
check.solution: She called herself Mrs Birling, which Mrs Birling took as an insolent use of her own name and which prejudiced her against the case. It is the third name the girl has used in the play, after Eva Smith and Daisy Renton, and the one that turns Mrs Birling's own son into the missing father.
options: Eva Smith
Sheila Croft
Mrs Birling
Daisy Renton

steps.title: Act 3: Eric, the speech, the telephone
steps.body:
**Eric's link.** He met the girl drunk in the same Palace bar, forced his way into her rooms, and went on seeing her. When she told him she was pregnant he gave her money he had taken from his father's office, and she refused it once she knew it was stolen. He is bitter with his father, “You're not the kind of father a chap could go to” (Eric, Act 3), and horrified when he learns that his mother turned the girl away.

**The speech.** The Inspector stops the family quarrel and sums up: “each of you helped to kill her” (the Inspector, Act 3). There are “millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths”. “We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” (the Inspector, Act 3). If that lesson is not learned, “they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish”. He leaves.

**The doubt.** With him gone, the family begins to pick at the evening. Gerald comes back having asked a police sergeant: there is no Inspector Goole on the force. Perhaps the photograph was of different girls. A telephone call to the Infirmary finds no suicide that night. Birling, his wife and Gerald relax; Gerald offers Sheila the ring again with “What about this ring?”. Sheila and Eric will not have it: “you don't seem to have learnt anything” (Sheila, Act 3).

**The telephone.** It rings. A girl has just died on her way to the Infirmary after swallowing disinfectant, and a police inspector is on his way to ask some questions. The curtain falls on the family staring at one another.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of the end of Act 3: the Inspector leaves, Gerald finds there is no Inspector Goole, the Infirmary reports no suicide, the older Birlings and Gerald relax, Sheila and Eric stay ashamed, and the telephone rings

check.prompt: Put these five moments from Act 3 in the order the play presents them.
check.solution: Eric's confession comes first, because the Inspector has not finished. The speech and exit follow. Only with the Inspector gone can Gerald return with the sergeant's news, which prompts the call to the Infirmary. The final telephone call is the last thing in the play. The order matters: every doubt is raised after the Inspector has left, so nothing he said is ever contradicted to his face.

steps.title: The chain, in order
steps.body: The Inspector's inquiry has a shape, and the shape is an argument. He takes the five people one at a time, in the order in which they met the girl, and he does not move on until the link is admitted. Watch what each link adds.

visuals.problem: Set out the five links in the order the play reveals them, and say what each one adds to the case.

steps.text: 1. Mr Birling sacked her from his works after she led a strike for higher wages.
steps.note: Employment: the first door shut in her face, by the man with most power over her.

steps.text: 2. Sheila had her sacked from Milwards, the shop, out of jealousy.
steps.note: A second door shut by a whim, and the first confession that admits harm was done.

steps.text: 3. Gerald met her as Daisy Renton in the Palace bar, kept her in a friend's rooms over the summer, then ended it.
steps.note: Rescue that was also use: the girl without work becomes a girl kept, then dropped.

steps.text: 4. Mrs Birling as chair of the women's charity committee, refused her help when she was pregnant and calling herself Mrs Birling.
steps.note: The last public source of help closed, by the person whose job was to open it.

steps.text: 5. Eric met her drunk in the Palace bar, forced his way in, made her pregnant and gave her money taken from his father's office, which she refused once she knew it was stolen.
steps.note: The private wrong behind the public one, and the money she would not take.

steps.text: Each link is worse than a single act of unkindness because of the one before it.
steps.note: That is what the Inspector means by a chain: no one of them killed her, and each of them helped to.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of the chain of events from Eva Smith at the works, through Birling, Sheila, Gerald, Mrs Birling and Eric, to the Infirmary

check.prompt: The Inspector questions one person at a time and shows the photograph to one person at a time. What does that structure do for the play?
check.solution: Taking the five one at a time means every link is admitted in front of the others before the next is opened, so a general denial, such as a claim that it was all different girls, is only possible once the Inspector has gone. The one-at-a-time photograph is what makes that later doubt possible, and Priestley uses both: the method proves the chain, and the trick leaves a loophole for the people who want one.

markScheme.description: Each link is proved and admitted before the next, so nobody can hide inside a general denial

options: It keeps the Inspector on stage for as long as possible before the doubts about him begin
It lets the family compare their memories of the photograph and agree on what it showed
It gives each character a scene of their own so that the actors share the stage time equally

steps.title: Time on stage: one room, one evening, three cliffhangers
steps.body:
The play runs in continuous time. The curtain falls twice and rises again on the same moment, so nothing happens off stage that the audience does not see. That choice makes the evening feel like a trial, and it lets Priestley end each act on a question.

**Act 1** ends with the discovery that the name Daisy Renton means something to Gerald. **Act 2** ends when the family realise who the father must be, and Eric enters. **Act 3** ends with the telephone. Each curtain is a cliffhanger, and the last one is the largest: the whole evening is about to happen again.

**Two clocks.** The characters live by the clock of 1912. The audience of 1945 lives by another. When Birling says the Titanic cannot sink, or that the Germans do not want war, the audience hears a man being wrong about the next thirty years, and by the time the Inspector arrives it has already stopped trusting him. The technical name for that gap is dramatic irony, and here it is built into the date on the programme.

columns: The question the audience is left holding
rows: Gerald reacts to the name Daisy Renton
What did Gerald have to do with her?
The father is understood to be Eric, and Eric walks in
What did Eric do, and does his mother know?
The telephone: a girl has died and an inspector is coming
Was any of it real, and will they live through it again?

check.prompt: Birling says the Titanic is unsinkable and that there will be no war. Why is this dramatic irony rather than simply a mistake?
check.solution: Dramatic irony is the gap between what the audience knows and what the characters know. Priestley set the play in 1912 and wrote it in 1945, so every confident forecast Birling makes had already failed by the time anyone watched it. The characters cannot know; the audience cannot help knowing. The irony is a structural choice made with the date, not a slip by a character.

markScheme.description: The audience of 1945 knows he is wrong about both, and the characters of 1912 cannot

steps.title: Which act, whose link?
steps.body:
Closed book means the plot is yours to carry in. Try these from memory before you look back.

1. Which two characters met Eva Smith in the Palace bar, and which of them met her first?
2. Which name did she use with Gerald, and which with the charity committee?
3. What does the family find out about Inspector Goole after he has gone, and who finds it out?
4. Which two characters refuse to be comforted by that discovery?

Then say the chain aloud, in order, with one sentence for each link. If you can do that, you have the spine of every essay on this play.

check.prompt: Where did both Gerald and Eric first meet the girl?
check.solution: The bar of the Palace, the local music hall. Gerald met her there as Daisy Renton and took her away from it; Eric met her there later, drunk. Priestley sends both young men to the same bar so that the audience sees one girl and two very different kinds of rescue.

steps.title: Structure is a method: writing about it for AO2
steps.body:
Twelve of the thirty marks for the essay are for the writer's methods, and structure is a method. Students who write about it well do three things.

**Name the choice.** Not *the play has a twist* but *Priestley delays the doubt about the Inspector until after his exit*. Not *the play is in real time* but *the action is continuous, so the family never leave the room in which they were comfortable*.

**Say what it does to the audience.** The delayed doubt means the speech about fire and blood is heard without any hint that its speaker might be a fraud; the audience takes it straight, and only afterwards watches the family try to wriggle out of it. The continuous time means there is no relief and nowhere to go.

**Tie it to the purpose.** The chain is the argument: responsibility is shared. The ending that begins again is the argument too: a lesson refused will be taught again. When a structural point ends with what Priestley wanted a 1945 audience to think, it is doing AO2 and AO3 work in one sentence.

check.prompt: Which sentence about the ending would earn AO2 credit for analysing structure?
check.solution: The sentence about delaying the doubt names a structural choice, says what it does to the audience, and connects it to the purpose: the doubt tests the family, not the message. The others retell the ending as a twist, guess that the Inspector was a ghost, or describe the curtain coming down. Retelling is AO1 at best; a structural choice with its effect is AO2.

The ending is a twist, because the telephone rings and a girl has died and an inspector is coming to ask questions, which is a complete surprise for the family on stage and for everyone watching in the theatre

steps.title: The play in one page
steps.body:
One room, one evening, 1912, written in 1945. A dinner to celebrate an engagement; a doorbell; an inspector with a photograph. Then doubt, relief for the three who want it, refusal from the two who do not, and a telephone that starts the evening again.

- **The chain:** Birling, Sheila, Gerald, Mrs Birling, Eric, in the order they met the girl, each link admitted before the next.
- **The names:** Eva Smith at the works and at Milwards; Daisy Renton with Gerald; Mrs Birling at the committee.
- **The curtains:** Act 1 on the name Daisy Renton; Act 2 on the realisation about Eric; Act 3 on the telephone.
- **The ending:** no Inspector Goole, no suicide at the Infirmary, relief, then a girl has died and an inspector is on his way.
- **The dates:** set in 1912, written in 1945, so every forecast Birling makes is dramatic irony.

Carry the order, the three names, the places and the ending into the exam. Everything else in this unit hangs on them.

questions.prompt: In which town is *An Inspector Calls* set?
questions.solution: Brumley, an industrial town in the north Midlands that Priestley invented so that it could stand for any manufacturing town of 1912. Priestley was born in Bradford, which is real, and Brumley is not.

questions.prompt: The Inspector says the young woman died after drinking something. What was it?
questions.solution: Disinfectant. The detail is stated at the start, and repeated in the last telephone call at the end, so that the final report of a girl who has just died after swallowing disinfectant matches exactly what the Inspector first told the family.

questions.prompt: Who is the first person the Inspector links to the girl, and why?
questions.solution: Mr Birling comes first, because he met her first: she worked at his works, helped lead a strike for higher wages, and was sacked when it failed. The Inspector's order is the order of her life, and Birling's sacking is the first door shut.

questions.solution: The play is set in spring 1912, the year the Titanic sailed and sank, and two years before the war Birling says will never come. Priestley wrote it in 1945, thirty-three years later, and the distance between the two dates is where the dramatic irony lives.

questions.prompt: Put the five people in the order in which they met the girl, which is also the order the Inspector questions them.
questions.solution: Birling sacked her from the works; Sheila had her dismissed from Milwards; Gerald met her in the Palace bar and kept her over the summer; Mrs Birling refused her when she was pregnant; Eric, who had met her after Gerald, was the father. The Inspector follows her life in order, and the play follows the Inspector.

questions.prompt: What name did the girl use when she applied to the charity committee, and whose name was it really?
questions.solution: She called herself Mrs Birling, the name of the woman who chaired the committee and who then refused her. Mrs Birling took it as impertinence and admits it prejudiced her against the girl's case; the audience later sees why the girl had a claim to the name.

questions.prompt: Why did Mrs Birling refuse the girl's appeal to the committee?
questions.solution: The girl used the name Mrs Birling, which the real Mrs Birling took as an insult, and she admits that it prejudiced her against the case; she then used her influence to have help refused. Priestley makes the reason petty on purpose: a life turns on a woman being offended by a name.

questions.prompt: The doubt about whether Inspector Goole is real is raised only after he has left the stage. What is the effect of that ordering on the audience?
questions.solution: Because nobody doubts Goole while he is on stage, the audience takes the speech about members of one body at face value. The doubt afterwards cannot undo what it has heard; it can only show which characters want an excuse. Priestley orders it that way so that the doubt tests the family, not the message.

questions.solution: Birling calls the Titanic unsinkable, and it sank on its maiden voyage in April 1912, within weeks of the evening of the play. He also says the Germans do not want war, and the audience of 1945 has just lived through the second war since he spoke. Both are dramatic irony built from the date.

questions.prompt: After the Inspector has gone and the Infirmary reports no suicide, which two characters refuse to treat that as letting the family off?
questions.solution: Sheila and Eric. The older Birlings and Gerald treat the discovery that there is no Inspector Goole and no suicide as the end of the matter; the two younger Birlings insist that what each of them did was done whether or not the girl was one girl. Priestley splits the family by generation, and the split is the play's hope.

questions.prompt: Put these four stages of the ending in the order Priestley arranges them, from the moment the Inspector leaves.
questions.solution: Doubt grows in steps: first the family's own questions, then Gerald's news, then the Infirmary call that seems to settle it. Only when relief is complete does the telephone ring. The order is a ladder of false comfort, and each rung makes the last call harder to bear.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Priestley uses the ending of *An Inspector Calls* to reinforce the play's message. Name the structural choices, say what they do to the audience, and connect them to what Priestley wanted a 1945 audience to think.
questions.solution: Priestley builds the ending as a ladder of false comfort and then kicks it away. Once the Inspector has left, the doubt about him grows in steps: the family's own questions, Gerald's news from the sergeant that there is no Inspector Goole, and the call to the Infirmary that finds no suicide. Each step lets Birling, his wife and Gerald relax a little more, until Gerald can offer Sheila the ring again. The audience, which heard the final speech without any suspicion because the doubt was delayed until after the Inspector's exit, watches the three of them talk themselves out of everything it has just taken to heart. Sheila's protest that they do not seem to have learnt anything is the audience's own thought spoken on stage. Then the telephone rings, a girl has died, and an inspector is on his way: the evening is about to happen again. The structure carries the argument. A lesson refused is repeated, exactly as the Inspector promised in the speech about fire and blood and anguish, and a 1945 audience that had lived through two wars since 1912 knew what being taught again felt like.

questions.modelAnswer: Priestley builds the ending as a ladder of false comfort and then kicks it away. Once the Inspector has left, the doubt about him grows in steps: the family's own questions, Gerald's news from the sergeant that there is no Inspector Goole, and the call to the Infirmary that finds no suicide. Each step lets Birling, his wife and Gerald relax a little more, until Gerald can offer Sheila the ring again. questions.prompt: The Inspector questions the five characters one at a time, in the order in which they met the girl. Write one analytical paragraph on how this chain works as a structural method, and what it makes the audience understand about responsibility.
questions.solution: Priestley makes the Inspector work in the order of the girl's life: Birling sacks her from the works, Sheila has her dismissed from Milwards, Gerald keeps her over the summer and drops her, Mrs Birling refuses her help, Eric leaves her pregnant with money she will not take. Each person is questioned separately and the photograph is shown to one at a time, so a link is admitted in front of the whole family before the next is opened. The order is what turns five separate unkindnesses into one chain. Sheila's jealousy would have been a small cruelty if the girl had still had her first job; it becomes the second door shut because Birling has already shut the first. Mrs Birling's refusal is the last public help closed after the private help from Gerald has been withdrawn. That is what the Inspector means when he says that each of them helped to kill her: no one of them did it, and the responsibility is not divided five ways but shared whole by each. Priestley wanted an audience in 1945, choosing what kind of country to rebuild, to understand responsibility that way, and the structure of the inquiry is the argument made visible.

questions.prompt: The Inspector shows the photograph to one person at a time. After he has gone, Gerald suggests it might have been a different girl each time. Why does Priestley give the family this loophole?
questions.solution: The loophole is a test. Whether the girl was one girl or five, each character did what they did, and the two younger Birlings say so. The three who seize on the doubt show the audience what they are. Priestley builds the loophole into the method so that the last scene can sort the family by what they choose to believe.

questions.prompt: A student writes: "The play happens in real time, so it is realistic, like watching a real dinner party." What is the better account of the continuous time?
questions.solution: Continuous time is a choice, and its effect is pressure, not realism: nobody leaves, nothing happens off stage, and the room that was the setting for a celebration becomes the setting for an inquiry without a change of scene. The student has noticed the method and stopped before its effect; the effect is where the marks are.

markScheme.description: Continuous time keeps the family in the one room where they were comfortable, with no relief and no exit, so the evening feels like a trial

options: Continuous time keeps the family in the one room where they were comfortable, with no relief and no exit, so the evening feels like a trial
Continuous time is a limitation of the theatre in 1945, when scene changes were expensive and slow and most new plays avoided them altogether
Continuous time makes the play realistic, and realism is what a 1945 audience expected from a drama
Continuous time was chosen so that the play could be performed without an interval

examTechnique.body:
**There is no extract for this text.** Paper 2 Section A gives two essay questions on *An Inspector Calls* and no printed passage, so every reference comes from memory. The chain in order, the three names, the act endings and the ending sequence are the minimum to carry in.

**Plot questions are structure questions in disguise.** A question on a character or a theme still pays twelve marks for methods, and the way Priestley orders the inquiry, ends the acts and delays the doubt is method. One paragraph on structure belongs in every essay on this play.

**Retelling earns almost nothing.** The bottom level of the mark scheme is narrative or descriptive in approach. Every paragraph should say what a choice does, not what happens next.

**Use the dates.** Set in 1912, written in 1945: a sentence on why Priestley chose that gap is context that explains a method, which is what AO3 wants.
examinerErrors: Retelling the plot in order, which the mark scheme places at the bottom level as narrative in approach.
Getting the chain out of order, which breaks any argument about the girl being pushed from one door to the next.
Calling the ending a twist and stopping there, with no account of what the delayed doubt and the telephone do to the audience.
Treating the continuous time as realism rather than as pressure.
Confusing the three names, or which name belongs with which link.
Saying the Inspector was proved not to exist, when the play leaves it open and the point is what each character chooses to believe.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats the plot as something Priestley built rather than something that happened. It names the order of the inquiry and shows how the order changes the meaning of each link; it knows where the acts end and what each curtain leaves the audience holding; it sees that the doubt about the Inspector is placed after his exit so that the speech is heard straight; and it reads the telephone as the play's argument, a lesson refused and repeated, put in front of an audience in 1945 that had just been taught twice. Quotations are short, exact and from the right act, and every one is followed by what it does.
